channel.title: Lacquer — CoProducer Journal
channel.description: Answer-first essays on loudness, true peak, repair, stems, ScrewAI, and local .bat workflows.

item.title: How loud should the vocal sit? Measure it against the beat
item.description: There’s no single right vocal level, but the vocal-to-beat loudness gap in LU is measurable. Match it to a reference, then fix only the buried bars.

item.title: Harsh S’s get louder after mastering. De-ess before the limiter
item.description: Vocals harsh after mastering? The master lifts level and top end, so borderline sibilance pops and eats true-peak headroom. Find the worst S’s and fix them in the mix.

item.title: Why streaming platforms turn loud masters down
item.description: Streaming services normalize toward −14 LUFS (Apple closer to −16). A hotter master is turned down, not played louder. Measure integrated LUFS before you limit again.

item.title: True peak is what codecs clip
item.description: True peak (dBTP) estimates inter-sample peaks. Streaming wants about −1.0 dBTP. A legal sample peak can still clip after AAC or Opus reconstruction.

item.title: What a 70-to-90 CoProducer repair actually changes
item.description: Public A/B proofs: Crazy Stacy 70→90 (831 clips→0), BeatGoHard 77→95, Drippin 66→93. A delivery pass — not a remix or taste rewrite.

item.title: Should you upload an unreleased master to the cloud?
item.description: Upload an unreleased master only if you accept a vendor holding the file. Loudness, true peak, and clip checks can stay fully local with CoProducer.

item.title: A release checklist that matches the meter
item.description: Release checklist: −14 LUFS ±1.5, true peak ≤ −1.0 dBTP, 0 clipped samples, ≥44.1 kHz, phase ≥ 0.2, score ≥ 90. Same gates CoProducer scores.

item.title: Crest factor is not loudness
item.description: Crest factor is peak-to-RMS height. LUFS is perceived loudness over time. You can raise crest and still miss −14 LUFS — or hit −14 with a crushed crest.

item.title: Phase correlation is a mono audition
item.description: Phase near 0 or negative means the mix thins or cancels in mono. CoProducer fails values under about 0.2. Auto-repair will not flip polarity for you.

item.title: Quiet masters get turned up — and so does the noise
item.description: Streaming turn-up lifts quiet files. A −20 LUFS master may be gained up, which also lifts hiss, rumble, and room tone. Quiet is not a free pass.

item.title: When not to reach for the limiter
item.description: Skip another limiter when clips are already non-zero, LUFS is only slightly hot, or the real problem is arrangement, noise, or a bad edit — not peak height.

item.title: Sample rate and bit depth are delivery hygiene
item.description: CoProducer fails sample rates under 44.1 kHz. Why 32 kHz fails delivery, when 44.1/48/96 are fine, what bit depth distributors want, and how to verify the bounce.

item.title: Reference matching without guesswork
item.description: Reference matching means comparing meters, not vibes. CoProducer’s divergence table shows where your bounce sits versus a reference on real gates.

item.title: Album consistency is a batch problem
item.description: Album consistency means every track clears the same delivery gates and sits in a similar loudness lane — a batch measurement problem, not one “final” bounce.

item.title: Why HTML, JSON, and TXT all matter
item.description: HTML is for humans and clients. JSON is for pipelines. TXT is for quick notes and tickets. CoProducer writes all three so the same facts travel cleanly.

item.title: Local tools beat upload queues
item.description: Local .bat and desktop tools skip upload queues, retention policies, and per-track metering fees. Keep measurement, stems, and syrup renders on your machine.

item.title: Stems diagnose mixes — they do not replace them
item.description: Stem separation isolates parts so you can hear collisions. It does not invent a better arrangement. Use stems to diagnose, then fix the mix.

item.title: Screw tempo still needs a legal peak
item.description: Slowing a track for syrup aesthetics changes duration and crest, not true-peak law. A screwed render still needs ≤ −1.0 dBTP before upload.

item.title: Vertical video is a loudness trap
item.description: Shorts, Reels, and Stories normalize differently from music stores, but crushed dialog and clipped music still fail. Measure before you post vertical.

item.title: Mastering .bat versus opening the session
item.description: A mastering .bat is for trusted delivery passes on finished mixes. Open the session when arrangement, bad edits, or clipped vocals need real surgery.

item.title: How to read a CoProducer score
item.description: A CoProducer score ≥ 90 means release-ready against the tool’s gates — not a Grammy. Read the findings: a 70 with 831 clips is a different emergency than a 77.

item.title: Re-encoding eats true-peak headroom
item.description: Every lossy encode can invent new inter-sample peaks. Leaving only 0.1 dB of true-peak margin is how a ‘clean’ WAV becomes a clipped stream.
